lead: Every method and theorem of this unit also works for AC circuits in the sinusoidal steady state. Replace each sinusoidal source by its phasor and each element by its impedance, and the DC steps go through unchanged with complex numbers: mesh and nodal analysis (with supermesh, supernode and dependent sources), superposition, Thevenin and Norton, compensation and the rest. Two things are new. Phasors of different frequencies cannot be added, so superposition must then be done in the time domain. And maximum power needs a conjugate match, ZL = Zth*, because the load must cancel the source's reactance as well as match its resistance.
prereq: You need: phasors, impedance and RMS values (sinusoidal steady state), and the DC methods of this unit: mesh, nodal, Thevenin and Norton.

sections.h3: Phasors and impedances: the DC methods carry over

blocks.text: At one angular frequency ω (rad/s, ω = 2πf), a sinusoid is represented by a phasor, a complex number with the RMS value as its size and the phase as its angle: 20∠0° V. Each element becomes an impedance Z in ohms:

items: inductor: Z = jωL, a positive reactance (L in henry);
capacitor: Z = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC), a negative reactance (C in farad).

blocks.text: Here j = √(−1). KVL and KCL hold for phasors, and V = ZI replaces Ohm's law, so every DC method applies word for word. Mesh analysis gives a matrix of impedances, Z I = V, with self-impedances on the diagonal and minus the shared impedances off it. Nodal analysis gives Y V = I with admittances Y = 1/Z in siemens. A current source on a shared branch still makes a supermesh, a floating voltage source still makes a supernode, and a dependent source is still written in the phasor of its controlling variable. Only the arithmetic is complex: keep real and imaginary parts separate, and convert to polar form at the end.

To return to the time domain, an RMS phasor |V|∠θ means v(t) = √2|V|cos(ωt + θ). Some books use peak-value phasors; then the √2 is dropped and every average power picks up a factor ½. State which you use and keep to it.

sections.h3: Superposition with one or several frequencies

blocks.text: If all sources have the same frequency, superposition works on phasors: switch off all but one independent source (voltage source shorted, current source opened, dependent sources kept), solve, repeat, and add the phasors.

If the sources have different frequencies, a phasor at 50 Hz and a phasor at 150 Hz rotate at different rates and cannot be added. Solve one circuit per frequency, with the impedances recalculated at that frequency (an inductor is 3 times larger in reactance at 150 Hz than at 50 Hz, and a capacitor 3 times smaller). Turn each answer into a time function and add the time functions. A DC source is the case ω = 0: inductors become shorts and capacitors opens.

Average power, unlike instantaneous power, does add across different frequencies, because the cross terms between two different frequencies average to zero over time. It still does not add across sources of the same frequency.

sections.h3: Thevenin, Norton and maximum average power

blocks.text: At one frequency a linear AC network seen from two terminals is a phasor source V<sub>th</sub> (the open-circuit voltage) in series with Z<sub>th</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> + jX<sub>th</sub>, found with the independent sources switched off; or a Norton current I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/Z<sub>th</sub> in parallel with Z<sub>th</sub>. With dependent sources, use V<sub>oc</sub>/I<sub>sc</sub> or a test source, exactly as for DC.
A load Z<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>L</sub> + jX<sub>L</sub> draws |I| = |V<sub>th</sub>|/|Z<sub>th</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub>| and takes average power |I|²R<sub>L</sub>:

items: The reactance appears only in the denominator, so choose X<sub>L</sub> = −X<sub>th</sub> to make that term zero.
What is left is the DC problem, so R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>.
Together: Z<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> − jX<sub>th</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>*, the complex conjugate, and P<sub>max</sub> = |V<sub>th</sub>|²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) with RMS V<sub>th</sub>.

blocks.text: If the load can only be a resistor, the best value is R<sub>L</sub> = |Z<sub>th</sub>|, which gives less than P<sub>max</sub>. Millman's theorem uses admittances, V = ΣV<sub>k</sub>Y<sub>k</sub>/ΣY<sub>k</sub>; reciprocity holds for networks of R, L and C; and the compensation source becomes the phasor IΔZ.

examples.question: In the top circuit of Figure 2.8.1 (RMS phasors), a source 20∠0° V (+ at the top) is in the left branch, 4 Ω in the top-left branch, a capacitor of −j4 Ω in the shared middle branch, and the right branch is the load, 4 Ω in series with an inductor of j4 Ω. Find the mesh currents I₁ and I₂, the load voltage, and check the power balance.
steps: Mesh 1, clockwise: (4 − j4)I₁ − (−j4)I₂ = 20, that is (4 − j4)I₁ + j4I₂ = 20.
Mesh 2, clockwise: −(−j4)I₁ + (−j4 + 4 + j4)I₂ = 0, that is j4I₁ + 4I₂ = 0, so I₂ = −jI₁.
I₂ = −j(2 + j1) = 1 − j2 A. In polar form I₁ = 2.236∠26.6° A and I₂ = 2.236∠−63.4° A.
Capacitor current (downward) I₁ − I₂ = 1 + j3 A = 3.162∠71.6° A.
Power check: the source delivers P = Re(V I₁*) = Re(20(2 − j1)) = 40 W. The resistors take |I₁|² × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20 W and |I₂|² × 4 = 20 W, total 40 W. The capacitor and inductor take no average power.
examples.answer: I₁ = 2 + j1 A = 2.236∠26.6° A, I₂ = 1 − j2 A = 2.236∠−63.4° A; load voltage 12 − j4 V; 40 W delivered and absorbed.

examples.question: For the same circuit, find the Thevenin equivalent seen by the load, check the load current against worked example 1, and find the load for maximum average power and that power.
steps: Remove the load. Open-circuit voltage across the capacitor by voltage division: V<sub>th</sub> = 20 × (−j4)/(4 − j4) = −j80(4 + j4)/32 = (320 − j320)/32 = 10 − j10 V = 14.14∠−45° V.
Switch off the source (short it): the load terminals see 4 Ω in parallel with −j4 Ω. Z<sub>th</sub> = 4(−j4)/(4 − j4) = −j16(4 + j4)/32 = (64 − j64)/32 = 2 − j2 Ω.
Norton check: I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/Z<sub>th</sub> = (10 − j10)/(2 − j2) = 5 A, which is the short-circuit current 20/4 = 5 A (a short across the capacitor leaves only the 4 Ω).
Conjugate match: Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>* = 2 + j2 Ω.
P<sub>max</sub> = |V<sub>th</sub>|²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) = 200/8 = 25 W. The original load 4 + j4 Ω takes |1 − j2|² × 4 = 20 W.
examples.answer: V<sub>th</sub> = 10 − j10 V (14.14∠−45° V), Z<sub>th</sub> = 2 − j2 Ω; the conjugate load 2 + j2 Ω takes 25 W, against 20 W for the original load.

traps: Matching R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> and ignoring the reactance. The reactances must cancel too: Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>*, not Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>.
Adding phasors of different frequencies. Solve each frequency separately and add the time functions.
Mixing peak and RMS phasors. P<sub>max</sub> = |V<sub>th</sub>|²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) needs RMS; with a peak phasor it is |V<sub>th</sub>|²/(8R<sub>th</sub>).
Keeping one reactance value at every frequency. X<sub>L</sub> = ωL and X<sub>C</sub> = −1/(ωC) must be recalculated for each frequency.
Adding magnitudes instead of complex numbers: |2 + j1| + |1 − j2| is not |(2 + j1) + (1 − j2)|.

quiz.q: What is the AC Thevenin equivalent of a linear network at one frequency?
quiz.a: A phasor voltage source V<sub>th</sub>, the open-circuit voltage, in series with an impedance Z<sub>th</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> + jX<sub>th</sub> found with the independent sources switched off.

quiz.q: Why can you not add the phasor responses of a 50 Hz source and a 150 Hz source?
quiz.a: A phasor stands for a sinusoid at one fixed frequency; the two rotate at different rates, so their sum is not a phasor at either frequency. Convert each to a time function and add those.

quiz.q: A source 20∠0° V RMS has a series impedance 4 + j3 Ω and a shunt impedance 4 − j3 Ω across the output. Find V<sub>th</sub> and Z<sub>th</sub>.
In worked example 2 the load may only be a resistor. What value takes the most power, and how much?
quiz.a: R<sub>L</sub> = |Z<sub>th</sub>| = 2.828 Ω. P = 200 × 2.828/[(2 + 2.828)² + 2²] = 565.7/27.31 = 20.71 W, below the 25 W of the conjugate match.

quiz.q: A load of 5 Ω is connected to V<sub>th</sub> = 10 V RMS and Z<sub>th</sub> = 5 + j10 Ω. Is it taking maximum power? Find its power and the maximum possible.
quiz.a: No. |Z<sub>th</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub>|² = 10² + 10² = 200, so P = 100 × 5/200 = 2.5 W. A conjugate load 5 − j10 Ω would take 100/20 = 5 W.

beyond: Radio and microwave engineers design L-section and stub matching networks that turn an antenna's impedance into the conjugate of an amplifier's, and use the Smith chart to do it. A loudspeaker's impedance changes with frequency, so amplifiers are designed to drive it from a low output impedance rather than match it. Power engineers cancel reactance with capacitor banks (power-factor correction) to reduce current, not to transfer maximum power. Search for 'L-network impedance matching', 'Smith chart' and 'power factor correction'.
